issues.legal_issue: The permissibility of a residential scheme for weaker sections under the excess-land scheme depends on the development plan in force when the scheme is considered, not on the plan in force when the land first became subject to the ceiling regime or when the scheme was filed.
material_facts: The scheme proposed residential dwelling units for weaker sections on land that had been designated for open space and other non-residential purposes in the development plan in force when the authorities considered the scheme.
An earlier development plan had permitted residential use, and the approving authority treated that earlier plan as controlling.
The agreement between the landholder and the scheme proponent was principally directed at carrying out the residential scheme.
issues.conclusion: The development plan in force when the scheme is considered governs whether the proposed residential use is permissible. The scheme could not be approved contrary to the then-current reservation, and the authority’s approval was erroneous.
issues.legal_principle: Section 21 of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 does not displace state town-planning law. Section 2(h), Rule 11-A and condition 1 of Schedule 1-A require the construction to be consistent with the relevant development plan; the plan is the one in force when the scheme is considered. The state’s surrender of legislative power under Article 252 was limited to the ceiling subject and did not surrender its town-planning powers. Section 42 did not apply because there was no relevant inconsistency. Atia Mohammadi Begum v. State of U.P. was confined to quantification of vacant land and did not freeze town planning or development plans for schemes of this kind.

predicates.scheme_approval_review: The proceeding concerns review of an authority’s decision on a proposed scheme for using excess vacant land.
predicates.scheme_seeks_residential_housing: The proposed scheme provides for residential housing on the land.
predicates.current_plan_reserves_land_for_other_use: The development plan in force when the authority considers the scheme designates the land for a use other than the proposed housing.

issues.definition: When an excess-land scheme approval is under review, a residential scheme on land reserved for another use by the plan in force at consideration is not approvable.

issues.legal_issue: Repeal preserves only rights that had accrued before repeal, and it does not preserve a claimed right founded on an erroneous approval or create a right merely from a private agreement.
material_facts: The ceiling legislation was repealed while the dispute was pending.
The land had not vested in the government, and possession remained with the landholder.
The claimed right to proceed with the scheme depended on an approval that the Court found erroneous because the scheme conflicted with the development plan.
The agreement itself did not transfer title or give the scheme proponent possession of the land.
issues.conclusion: No relevant right had accrued to the scheme proponent before repeal, so the claimed right was not saved by the repeal or by the general savings rule.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3 of the repealing legislation did not save approvals under Section 21 of the repealed Act. Section 6 of the General Clauses Act preserves accrued rights unless a different intention appears, and a repeal does not automatically extinguish accrued rights. Bansidhar v. State of Rajasthan and I.T. Commissioner, U.P. v. Shah Sadiq & Sons support that principle. But no right was saved here: the agreement alone created no right to the statutory benefit, and the later approval was erroneous.

predicates.repeal_effect_dispute: The proceeding requires determination of whether repeal preserves a claimed right under the former legal regime.
predicates.claimed_right_depends_on_invalid_approva: The claimant bases the asserted right on an approval that was legally erroneous.
predicates.no_independent_accrued_right: The claimant had no independent accrued right apart from the erroneous approval, and had not obtained possession or title under the arrangement.

issues.definition: In a dispute about the effect of repeal, a claim resting only on an erroneous approval and unsupported by an independent accrued right is not preserved.

issues.legal_issue: A contract that permits unilateral rescission before delivery of possession is determinable, is not an agency coupled with an interest merely because the agent may prepare and pursue a scheme, and is not specifically enforceable as a qualifying building contract.
material_facts: The agreement provided that neither party could unilaterally rescind it after the scheme proponent had been put in possession.
The landholder had not delivered possession when the agreement was terminated by notice.
The scheme proponent had prepared and pursued applications but had obtained no possession or proprietary interest in the land.
The agreement concerned carrying out a statutory housing scheme and was not the type of building contract covered by the specific-performance exception relied on by the scheme proponent.
issues.conclusion: The agreement could be terminated unilaterally before possession was delivered; the agency was not coupled with an interest, and the agreement could not be specifically enforced as a determinable contract.
issues.legal_principle: Section 202 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 protects an agency only where the agent has an interest in the subject matter; preparatory steps and expenditure on a proposed scheme did not create such an interest here. The plain meaning of the unambiguous termination clause controlled, and the affidavit and subsequent conduct could not alter that meaning. Under Section 14(1)(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, a contract in its nature determinable cannot be specifically enforced. Section 14(3)(c) did not apply because this was not the relevant kind of building contract. The Court relied on The Central Bank of India Ltd. v. Hartford Fire Insurance Co. Ltd. in holding that a clear contractual right of termination is not invalid merely because it is absolute, and distinguished Godhra Electricity Co. Ltd. v. State of Gujarat and National Fertilizers v. Puran Chand Nangia.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and rescission_bar_begins_only_after_possession and possession_not_delivered and contract_terminated_before_possession and agent_has_no_interest_in_subject_matter

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.rescission_bar_begins_only_after_possess: The contract bars unilateral rescission only after the other party has been put in possession.
predicates.possession_not_delivered: The party seeking performance had not been put in possession when the dispute arose.
predicates.contract_terminated_before_possession: The other contracting party gave notice terminating the contract before possession was delivered.
predicates.agent_has_no_interest_in_subject_matter: The party pursuing the scheme acquired no interest in the land beyond authority to prepare and pursue the scheme.

issues.definition: In a specific-performance suit, a contract whose rescission bar begins only upon possession may be terminated before possession, and it is not specifically enforceable when the agent has no interest in the subject matter.

issues.legal_issue: A contract whose performance requires continuous supervision that the court cannot provide is not specifically enforceable.
material_facts: Performance required construction of many dwelling units and their subsequent allotment to eligible occupants.
The scheme required ongoing monitoring of construction and allotment.
After repeal of the governing legislation, the competent authority that might have supervised implementation no longer existed.
issues.conclusion: The contract involved continuous supervision that could not be undertaken by the court, and specific performance was unavailable on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14(1)(d) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 excludes specific performance where the contract requires performance of a continuous duty that the court cannot supervise. The Court also observed that, after repeal, supervision could not be assigned to the former competent authority because it was no longer in existence.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.performance_requires_continuous_supervis: Carrying out the contract requires ongoing supervision of construction, delivery, or allocation.
predicates.no_available_supervisory_authority: Neither the court nor an existing competent authority can provide the required supervision.

issues.definition: In a specific-performance suit, a duty requiring continuous supervision cannot be specifically enforced when no available institution can provide that supervision.

issues.legal_issue: Specific performance may be refused where enforcing the contract would be inequitable because its public purpose cannot be achieved, implementation is impracticable, or enforcement would confer an unjustified benefit.
material_facts: The development plan in force reserved the land for uses inconsistent with the proposed residential housing.
The scheme therefore could not provide the intended housing benefit to weaker sections under the applicable planning regime.
Construction and later allotment would be extremely difficult, if not impossible, to supervise.
The proposed use of a large area of land for a much smaller housing project risked an uncalled-for benefit to the scheme proponent.
The approval relied on to support enforcement was legally erroneous, and the governing legislation had been repealed.
issues.conclusion: It would be inequitable to maintain the decree for specific performance, and the Court refused that relief.
issues.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 makes specific performance discretionary and requires the discretion to be exercised on sound judicial principles. The Court relied on K. Narendra v. Riviera Apartments (P) Ltd. in assessing the impracticability of performance and the effect of failed development plans, and held that the failed public purpose, practical obstacles, possible bonanza, and erroneous approval made enforcement inequitable.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.public_purpose_cannot_be_achieved: The land-use restrictions prevent the contract from delivering its intended public benefit.
predicates.performance_is_impracticable: The proposed construction and subsequent allocation cannot feasibly be carried out or supervised.
predicates.enforcement_would_create_unjustified_ben: Enforcement would confer a substantial benefit on the claimant out of proportion to the project that can lawfully be carried out.

issues.definition: Specific performance is refused where, in a suit for that relief, the public purpose cannot be achieved, performance is impracticable, or enforcement would create an unjustified benefit.
